claim: Late-passage (passage 40 or greater) Tert-/- mESCs possess significantly shorter telomeres compared to WT mESCs.
source: To address the role of telomere shortening on stem cell differentiation, we analyzed late-passage (passage 40 or greater) Tert-/- mESCs that possess significantly shorter telomeres and an increase in end-to-end fusions compared to WT mESCs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B; Liu et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B showing Q-FISH analysis and by citation to Liu et al., 2000.

claim: Late-passage Tert-/- mESCs exhibit an increase in end-to-end fusions compared to WT mESCs.
source: To address the role of telomere shortening on stem cell differentiation, we analyzed late-passage (passage 40 or greater) Tert-/- mESCs that possess significantly shorter telomeres and an increase in end-to-end fusions compared to WT mESCs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B; Liu et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B and by citation to Liu et al., 2000.

claim: There was no observable difference in population doubling time between WT and Tert-/- mESC lines.
source: Despite this telomere instability, and consistent with our previously reported results, there was no observable difference in population doubling time between the lines (Pucci et al., 2013) (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Pucci et al., 2013 and reference to unpublished data.

claim: WT mESCs transition from a GFP+ state to a GFP- state after ATRA treatment and remain GFP- after LIF re-addition.
source: As expected after induction of differentiation (6 DA), WT mESCs went from a GFP+ state (green) to a GFP- state (blue) and remained so even after LIF re-addition (orange) (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B showing FACS analysis of Pou5f1-GFP reporter expression.

claim: Tert-/- mESCs fail to fully repress the GFP reporter when treated with ATRA.
source: In contrast, Tert-/- mESCs failed to fully repress the GFP reporter when treated with ATRA, and this defect became more pronounced after re-addition of LIF-containing media (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B showing FACS analysis of Pou5f1-GFP reporter expression.

claim: The failure of Tert-/- mESCs to repress Pou5f1-GFP during differentiation is reflected in higher endogenous levels of Pou5f1 and Nanog mRNA.
source: The failure of Tert-/- mESCs to repress Pou5f1 -GFP during differentiation was also reflected in higher endogenous levels of Pou5f1 and Nanog mRNA (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: GFP+ sorted sub-populations of Tert-/- mESCs retain a higher level of pluripotency gene expression after ATRA or LIF re-addition.
source: GFP cell-sorting and further analysis of other pluripotency markers showed that GFP+ sorted sub-populations of Tert-/- mESCs retained a higher level of pluripotency gene expression after ATRA (SA), or LIF re-addition (SL) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C showing heatmap of pluripotency gene expression.

claim: Gamma-irradiation up to 5 Gy does not affect the GFP status of WT mESCs grown in LIF or after differentiation.
source: We also found that gamma-irradiation up to 5 Gy did not affect the GFP status of WT mESCs grown in LIF or after differentiation, which argues against a general effect of DNA damage on differentiation commitment under these conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–H showing survival fraction and differentiation analysis of irradiated mESCs.

claim: Tert-/- mESCs are slightly less radio-sensitive than WT mESCs.
source: In contrast, Tert-/- mESCs, although slightly less radio-sensitive than WT mESCs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), exhibited a further defect in differentiation commitment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G,H).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E showing survival fraction after gamma-irradiation.

claim: Tert-/- mESCs exhibit a further defect in differentiation commitment after gamma-irradiation.
source: In contrast, Tert-/- mESCs, although slightly less radio-sensitive than WT mESCs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), exhibited a further defect in differentiation commitment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G,H).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G,H showing differentiation analysis of irradiated mESCs.

claim: DNA damage may enhance the impact of critically eroded telomeres on differentiation.
source: These results suggest that DNA damage may enhance the impact of critically eroded telomeres, but that the effect is not merely attributable to DNA damage per se.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing differential effects of irradiation on WT versus Tert-/- mESCs.

claim: The transcriptional profiles between undifferentiated WT and Tert-/- mESCs are more alike than other differentiated cell populations.
source: First, as anticipated the transcriptional profiles between undifferentiated WT and Tert-/- mESCs were more alike than other differentiated cell populations (Figure 1E, columns 1 and 2, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, circle 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by heatmap and PCA analysis shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: WT mESCs treated with ATRA form a distinct group relative to ATRA-treated Tert-/- mESCs based on transcriptional profiles.
source: Second, in keeping with the differences observed in pluripotency gene expression profiles, WT mESCs treated with ATRA formed a distinct group relative to ATRA-treated Tert-/- mESCs (Figure 1E, column 3 and 5–7, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,compare blue and orange triangles with circles 2, 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by heatmap and PCA analysis shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: There is a difference between Tert-/- mESCs sorted for GFP- or GFP+ status after ATRA and LIF treatment based on transcriptional profiles.
source: Third, within the populations treated with ATRA and LIF (6 DA + 6 DL) (Figure 1E, columns 4, 8–11), there was a difference between Tert-/- mESCs that were sorted for GFP- or GFP+ status (Figure 1E, column 4, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, circles 2 and 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by heatmap and PCA analysis shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: There are at least two distinct sub-populations within Tert-/- mESCs treated with ATRA, or ATRA and LIF.
source: These data suggest there are at least two distinct sub-populations within Tert-/- mESCs treated with ATRA, or ATRA and LIF: GFP+ populations in which pluripotency genes fail to be repressed (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), and GFP- populations whose transcriptional profiles differ from GFP- WT mESCs (Figure 1E, compare columns 3, 8 versus 4–6).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from transcriptional profiling data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Global H3K27me3 levels are upregulated in Tert-/- mESCs.
source: As we demonstrated previously using an antibody that we validated for its specificity against H3K27me3, global H3K27me3 levels were also upregulated in Tert-/- mESCs (Pucci et al., 2013; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and by citation to Pucci et al., 2013.

claim: Ezh2 mRNA is slightly lower in undifferentiated Tert-/- ESCs compared with WT ESCs.
source: Although Ezh2 mRNA was slightly lower in undifferentiated Tert-/- ESCs compared with WT ESCs, Ezh2, Suz12, and Eed continued to be expressed after differentiation at levels that did not significantly differ from WT ESCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Ezh2, Suz12, and Eed continue to be expressed after differentiation at levels that do not significantly differ between Tert-/- and WT ESCs.
source: Although Ezh2 mRNA was slightly lower in undifferentiated Tert-/- ESCs compared with WT ESCs, Ezh2, Suz12, and Eed continued to be expressed after differentiation at levels that did not significantly differ from WT ESCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Active PRC2 inhibitors reduce global H3K27me3 in WT and Tert-/- mESCs.
source: Western blot analysis showed that the active PRC2 inhibitors, but not their inactive analogues, reduced global H3K27me3 in WT and Tert-/- mESCs (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: mESCs maintained in LIF or treated with ATRA exhibit no significant alteration in Pou5f1-GFP expression upon treatment with PRC2 inhibitors or their inactive analogues.
source: Irrespective of genotype, mESCs maintained in LIF or treated with ATRA (6 DA) exhibited no significant alteration in the expression of Pou5f1-GFP upon treatment with PRC2 inhibitors or their inactive analogues, relative to DMSO-treated controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: PRC2 inhibition leads to a marked exacerbation of the differentiation defect in Tert-/- mESCs.
source: We found that PRC2 inhibition led to a marked exacerbation of the differentiation defect in Tert-/- mESCs.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence including FACS analysis and gene expression data.

claim: A significant increase in the percentage of GFP+ cells is observed in Tert-/- mESCs treated with PRC2 inhibitors for 14 days.
source: A significant increase in the percentage of GFP+ cells was observed in Tert-/- mESCs treated with PRC2 inhibitors for 14 days, compared with the inactive analogues or DMSO-treated cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Endogenous Nanog mRNA and protein expression are further increased in Tert-/- mESCs treated with PRC2 inhibitors relative to DMSO treatment.
source: The expression of endogenous Nanog mRNA or protein (Figure 2C, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F,G), and other pluripotency gene markers such as Gdf3, Lefty1 and Zfp42 were also further increased relative to Tert-/- mESCs treated with DMSO (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot and RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F,G.

claim: WT mESCs exhibit no significant increase in the percentage of GFP+ cells after 14 days of PRC2 inhibitor treatment relative to DMSO treatment.
source: In contrast, WT mESCs exhibited no significant increase in the percentage of GFP+ cells after 14 days of inhibitor relative to DMSO treatment (Figure 2B) and differentiation induction of WT mESCs led to a sustained downregulation of pluripotency factor expression (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 2B and protein/mRNA expression data in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F,G.

claim: PRC2 inhibition leads to an alteration in the overall gene expression profiles in Tert-/- mESCs after differentiation treatment.
source: Heatmap and principal component analysis showed that PRC2 inhibition also led to an alteration in the overall gene expression profiles in Tert-/- mESCs after treatment with the PRC2 inhibitors GSK343, UNC1999 and A395 compared with their inactive analogues (UNC2400, A395N) or DMSO treatment alone (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by heatmap and PCA analysis shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Kdm6b and Kdm6a mRNA levels are comparable in Tert-/- ESCs and WT ESCs.
source: We first assessed Kdm6b and Kdm6a (UTX) mRNA expression, and found that mRNA levels were comparable in Tert-/- ESCs and WT ESCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: GSKJ4 treatment leads to a significant reduction in the GFP+ population in Tert-/- mESCs compared with DMSO or GSKJ5 treatment.
source: Despite the modest and statistically insignificant impact of GSKJ4 treatment on global H3K27me3 levels (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), there was a significant reduction in the GFP+ population in Tert-/- mESCs compared with DMSO or GSKJ5 treatment, and no observable impact on WT mESCs (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: GSKJ4 treatment has no observable impact on the GFP+ population in WT mESCs.
source: Despite the modest and statistically insignificant impact of GSKJ4 treatment on global H3K27me3 levels (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), there was a significant reduction in the GFP+ population in Tert-/- mESCs compared with DMSO or GSKJ5 treatment, and no observable impact on WT mESCs (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Pou5f1, Nanog mRNA and protein, and other endogenous pluripotency markers are modestly repressed in GSKJ4-treated Tert-/- mESCs relative to DMSO-treated cells.
source: Quantitative PCR gene expression and western blot analysis showed that Pou5f1, Nanog mRNA and protein, and other endogenous pluripotency markers were modestly repressed in GSKJ4-treated Tert-/- mESCs relative to DMSO-treated cells (Figure 3C, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR and western blot data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: GSKJ4 treatment alters the overall transcriptional profile of Tert-/- mESCs.
source: Heatmap and principal component analysis revealed that GSKJ4 treatment altered the overall transcriptional profile of Tert-/- mESCs (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1G), whereas GSKJ5 and DMSO-treated cells were more similar to each other.
evidence: The claim is supported by heatmap and PCA analysis shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Ezh2 knockdown leads to a statistically significant impairment in differentiation in Tert-/- mESCs.
source: Neither gene-targetted population exhibited a difference in the differentiation capacity of WT mESCs, but in Tert-/- mESCs, Ezh2 knockdown led to a statistically significant impairment in differentiation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1L).
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1L.

claim: Kdm6b knockdown partially alleviates the differentiation defect in Tert-/- mESCs.
source: Conversely, Kdm6b knockdown partially alleviated this defect (Figure 3—figure supplement 1L).
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1L.

claim: Differentiated Tert-/- mESCs possess a distinct chromatin accessibility landscape compared to WT mESCs.
source: Spearman correlation between ATAC-seq profiles of mESC populations highlighted a distinct chromatin accessibility landscape in differentiated Tert-/- mESCs compared to WT mESCs.
evidence: The claim is supported by ATAC-seq analysis and Spearman correlation shown in Figure 4A.

claim: There is a high degree of similarity between all differentiated WT mESC samples with or without treatment with PRC2 or Kdm6a/b inhibitors.
source: In differentiated WT mESCs, there was a high degree of similarity between all samples with or without treatment with PRC2 or Kdm6a/b inhibitors (Figure 4A, samples 1–9).
evidence: The claim is supported by Spearman correlation analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Undifferentiated WT mESCs more closely resemble Tert-/- mESCs in chromatin accessibility profiles.
source: In contrast, undifferentiated WT mESCs more closely resembled Tert-/- mESCs (Figure 4A, samples 10–24).
evidence: The claim is supported by Spearman correlation analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: GSK343-treated Tert-/- mESCs are most similar to WT undifferentiated mESCs in chromatin accessibility profiles.
source: Of these latter Tert-/- mESC chromatin accessibility profiles, the GSK343-treated cells were most similar to WT undifferentiated mESCs (Figure 4A, samples 14–15).
evidence: The claim is supported by Spearman correlation analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Tert-/- mESCs treated with ATRA differ from WT mESCs treated with ATRA in chromatin accessibility profiles.
source: Consistent with the principal component analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), Tert-/- mESCs treated with ATRA alone also differed from WT mESCs treated with ATRA (Figure 4A, compare samples 1 versus 10–12), and clustered with GFP- Tert-/- mESCs treated with ATRA + LIF (Figure 4A, sample 13).
evidence: The claim is supported by Spearman correlation and PCA analysis shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The Pou5f1 promoter shows a transition from high to low accessible chromatin signal intensity in WT mESCs but not in Tert-/- mESCs.
source: These data were consistent with visual inspection of the ATAC-seq profiles within the Pou5f1 promoter, which showed a transition from high to low accessible chromatin signal intensity in WT mESCs but not in Tert-/- mESCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Spearman analysis of H3K27me3 ChIP-seq profiles shows that undifferentiated WT and Tert-/- mESCs are similar (Spearman coefficient = 0.4).
source: Consistent with the ATAC-seq results, Spearman analysis of the H3K27me3 ChIP-seq profiles between undifferentiated WT and Tert-/- mESCs showed they were similar (Spearman coefficient = 0.4), and possessed little H3K27me3 at the Pou5f1 promoter (Figure 4B, left panel, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq analysis shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Undifferentiated WT and Tert-/- mESCs possess little H3K27me3 at the Pou5f1 promoter.
source: Consistent with the ATAC-seq results, Spearman analysis of the H3K27me3 ChIP-seq profiles between undifferentiated WT and Tert-/- mESCs showed they were similar (Spearman coefficient = 0.4), and possessed little H3K27me3 at the Pou5f1 promoter (Figure 4B, left panel, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: After ATRA and LIF treatment in the presence of PRC2 inhibitors, WT mESCs cluster separately from Tert-/- mESCs in H3K27me3 ChIP-seq profiles.
source: After ATRA and LIF treatment in the presence of the PRC2 inhibitors GSK343 or UNC1999, the WT mESCs clustered separately from Tert-/- mESCs, in keeping with the ATAC-seq and transcriptional analysis.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Differentiated Tert-/- mESCs display a different pattern of H3K27me3 at the Pou5f1 promoter compared to WT mESCs.
source: The assigned ChIP-seq reads obtained from these differentiated mESC populations were insufficient to enable quantitation of chromatin-associated H3K27me3 at specific loci, however visual examination of the Pou5f1 promoter revealed that differentiated Tert-/- mESCs displayed a different pattern of H3K27me3 compared to WT mESCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), including subtly increased or broadened peaks, and a few regions with reduced H3K27me3 as we noted previously (region 35642672–35642810) (Pucci et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and by citation to Pucci et al., 2013.

claim: Eroded telomeres lead to differentiation instability in murine embryonic stem cells via DNA hypomethylation at pluripotency-factor promoters.
source: Previously, we showed that eroded telomeres lead to differentiation instability in murine embryonic stem cells (mESCs) via DNA hypomethylation at pluripotency-factor promoters.
evidence: The claim is based on previously published work by the authors.

claim: Tert-/- mESCs exhibit genome-wide alterations in chromatin accessibility during differentiation.
source: Here, we uncovered that telomerase reverse transcriptase null (Tert-/-) mESCs exhibit genome-wide alterations in chromatin accessibility and gene expression during differentiation.
evidence: The claim is supported by ATAC-seq and gene expression data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Tert-/- mESCs exhibit genome-wide alterations in gene expression during differentiation.
source: Here, we uncovered that telomerase reverse transcriptase null (Tert-/-) mESCs exhibit genome-wide alterations in chromatin accessibility and gene expression during differentiation.
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression array data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Alterations in chromatin accessibility and gene expression in Tert-/- mESCs are accompanied by an increase of H3K27me3 globally.
source: These changes were accompanied by an increase of H3K27me3 globally, an altered chromatin landscape at the Pou5f1/Oct4 promoter, and a refractory response to differentiation cues.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot and ChIP-seq data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Tert-/- mESCs exhibit an altered chromatin landscape at the Pou5f1/Oct4 promoter.
source: These changes were accompanied by an increase of H3K27me3 globally, an altered chromatin landscape at the Pou5f1/Oct4 promoter, and a refractory response to differentiation cues.
evidence: The claim is supported by ATAC-seq and ChIP-seq data at the Pou5f1 promoter.

claim: Tert-/- mESCs exhibit a refractory response to differentiation cues.
source: These changes were accompanied by an increase of H3K27me3 globally, an altered chromatin landscape at the Pou5f1/Oct4 promoter, and a refractory response to differentiation cues.
evidence: The claim is supported by differentiation assay data showing persistent GFP+ cells and pluripotency gene expression.

claim: Inhibition of PRC2 exacerbates the impairment in differentiation in Tert-/- mESCs but not wild-type mESCs.
source: Inhibition of the Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2), an H3K27 tri-methyltransferase, exacerbated the impairment in differentiation and pluripotency gene repression in Tert-/- mESCs but not wild-type mESCs, whereas inhibition of H3K27me3 demethylation led to a partial rescue of the Tert-/- phenotype.
evidence: The claim is supported by differentiation assays with PRC2 inhibitors shown in Figure 2.

claim: Inhibition of PRC2 exacerbates the impairment in pluripotency gene repression in Tert-/- mESCs but not wild-type mESCs.
source: Inhibition of the Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2), an H3K27 tri-methyltransferase, exacerbated the impairment in differentiation and pluripotency gene repression in Tert-/- mESCs but not wild-type mESCs, whereas inhibition of H3K27me3 demethylation led to a partial rescue of the Tert-/- phenotype.
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data with PRC2 inhibitors shown in Figure 2.

claim: Inhibition of H3K27me3 demethylation leads to a partial rescue of the Tert-/- phenotype.
source: Inhibition of the Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2), an H3K27 tri-methyltransferase, exacerbated the impairment in differentiation and pluripotency gene repression in Tert-/- mESCs but not wild-type mESCs, whereas inhibition of H3K27me3 demethylation led to a partial rescue of the Tert-/- phenotype.
evidence: The claim is supported by differentiation assays with Kdm6a/b inhibitors shown in Figure 3.

claim: There is a new interdependent relationship between H3K27me3 and telomere integrity in stem cell lineage commitment.
source: These data reveal a new interdependent relationship between H3K27me3 and telomere integrity in stem cell lineage commitment that may have implications in aging and cancer.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing differential effects of H3K27me3 modulation in Tert-/- versus WT mESCs.

claim: The capacity of pluripotent or multipotent cells to replenish committed cell lineages deteriorates with age due to intrinsic and extrinsic factors.
source: The capacity of these cells to replenish committed cell lineages deteriorates with age due to intrinsic and extrinsic factors (Liu and Rando, 2011; Waterstrat and Van Zant, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Liu and Rando, 2011 and Waterstrat and Van Zant, 2009.

claim: Neuronal or melanocyte stem cell numbers significantly decline with age.
source: For example, neuronal or melanocyte stem cell numbers significantly decline with age, whereas aging of hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) leads to aberrant lineage specification and defects in cell fate determination (Krauss and de Haan, 2016; Maslov et al., 2004; Molofsky et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Krauss and de Haan, 2016; Maslov et al., 2004; Molofsky et al., 2006.

claim: Aging of hematopoietic stem cells leads to aberrant lineage specification and defects in cell fate determination.
source: For example, neuronal or melanocyte stem cell numbers significantly decline with age, whereas aging of hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) leads to aberrant lineage specification and defects in cell fate determination (Krauss and de Haan, 2016; Maslov et al., 2004; Molofsky et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Krauss and de Haan, 2016; Maslov et al., 2004; Molofsky et al., 2006.

claim: Telomere erosion occurs in cells that lack sufficient activity of telomerase.
source: Telomere erosion occurs in cells that lack sufficient activity of an enzyme called telomerase, whose catalytic core is comprised of a reverse transcriptase (TERT) and an integral RNA component (TR).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about telomerase function.

claim: Without telomerase, telomere decline eventually leads to telomere uncapping.
source: Without telomerase, an inexorable decline in telomere reserves eventually leads to what is termed telomere uncapping.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about telomere biology.

claim: Telomere uncapping elicits a DNA damage response that results in chromosome loss, rearrangements, and cell death or arrest.
source: This uncapping elicits a DNA damage response that results in chromosome loss, rearrangements, and cell death or arrest (de Lange, 2018; Lazzerini-Denchi and Sfeir, 2016; Muraki et al., 2012; Takai et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to de Lange, 2018; Lazzerini-Denchi and Sfeir, 2016; Muraki et al., 2012; Takai et al., 2003.

claim: Mice heterozygous for Terc or Tert are haploinsufficient for telomere maintenance.
source: Mice heterozygous for the genes encoding the telomerase RNA (Terc) or telomerase reverse transcriptase (Tert) are haploinsufficient for telomere maintenance and, depending on the genetic background, eventually exhibit many of the stem cell defects associated with telomerase knockout strains (Harrington, 2012; Strong et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Harrington, 2012; Strong et al., 2011.

claim: Telomere erosion occurs in human stem cells during aging, despite the persistence of low levels of telomerase activity.
source: Similar telomere erosion occurs in human stem cells during aging, despite the persistence of low levels of telomerase activity (Baerlocher et al., 2007; Lansdorp, 2008; Röth et al., 2003; Vaziri et al., 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Baerlocher et al., 2007; Lansdorp, 2008; Röth et al., 2003; Vaziri et al., 1994.

claim: Shorter telomeres are associated with dyskeratosis congenita, aplastic anemia, lung fibrosis, and blood cancer.
source: Although a causal link between short telomeres and human aging is still under investigation, shorter telomeres are associated with many human disorders that include dyskeratosis congenita, aplastic anemia, lung fibrosis, and blood cancer (Adams et al., 2015; Armanios and Blackburn, 2012; Blackburn et al., 2015; Decottignies and d'Adda di Fagagna, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Adams et al., 2015; Armanios and Blackburn, 2012; Blackburn et al., 2015; Decottignies and d'Adda di Fagagna, 2011.

claim: Disorders associated with short telomeres are marked by failures in cell differentiation.
source: These disorders are marked by failures in cell differentiation (Fu et al., 2018; Lo Sardo et al., 2017), and by stem cell depletion in the blood and other tissues (Bertuch, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fu et al., 2018; Lo Sardo et al., 2017.

claim: Disorders associated with short telomeres are marked by stem cell depletion in the blood and other tissues.
source: These disorders are marked by failures in cell differentiation (Fu et al., 2018; Lo Sardo et al., 2017), and by stem cell depletion in the blood and other tissues (Bertuch, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bertuch, 2016.

claim: DNA methylation patterns are altered during aging, whereby the genome becomes largely hypomethylated with hypermethylation at some loci.
source: For example, DNA methylation patterns are altered during aging, whereby the genome becomes largely hypomethylated with hypermethylation at some loci (Krauss and de Haan, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Krauss and de Haan, 2016.

claim: DNA methyltransferase activity is downregulated with age.
source: One contributing mechanism may be the downregulation of DNA methyltransferase (Dnmt) activity with age (Sun et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Sun et al., 2014.

claim: DNA hypomethylation does not affect stem cell self-renewal capacity nor the expression of pluripotency genes.
source: Despite the finding that DNA hypomethylation does not affect stem cell self-renewal capacity nor the expression of pluripotency genes (Beerman and Rossi, 2015), Dnmt3a knock-out mice exhibit an increase in HSC self-renewal and a predisposition to hematopoietic malignancies (Mayle et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Beerman and Rossi, 2015.

claim: Dnmt3a knock-out mice exhibit an increase in HSC self-renewal and a predisposition to hematopoietic malignancies.
source: Despite the finding that DNA hypomethylation does not affect stem cell self-renewal capacity nor the expression of pluripotency genes (Beerman and Rossi, 2015), Dnmt3a knock-out mice exhibit an increase in HSC self-renewal and a predisposition to hematopoietic malignancies (Mayle et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Mayle et al., 2015.

claim: Decreased tri-methylation of histone H3 on lysine 27 (H3K27me3) is associated with and may help drive the onset of senescence.
source: Changes in the abundance of other epigenetic modifications, such as decreased tri-methylation of histone H3 on lysine 27 (H3K27me3) is associated with and may help drive the onset of senescence (Ito et al., 2018; Shah et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ito et al., 2018; Shah et al., 2013.

claim: An increase of H3K27me3 in HSCs and muscle stem cells observed in aged mice is suggested to restrict stem cell potential via a differentiation bias of older stem cells.
source: Conversely, an increase of H3K27me3 in HSCs and muscle stem cells observed in aged mice is suggested to restrict stem cell potential via a differentiation bias of older stem cells (Brunet and Rando, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Brunet and Rando, 2017.

claim: Loss of telomere integrity affects chromatin throughout the telomeric and sub-telomeric DNA in mice.
source: In mice, loss of telomere integrity affects chromatin throughout the telomeric and sub-telomeric DNA (Benetti et al., 2008; Benetti et al., 2007; Gonzalo et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Benetti et al., 2008; Benetti et al., 2007; Gonzalo et al., 2006.

claim: The telomere shelterin subunit Rap1 has roles distal to the telomere in mice and in budding yeast.
source: More recently, roles distal to the telomere have been described for the telomere shelterin subunit, Rap1, in mice and in budding yeast (Marión et al., 2017; Platt et al., 2013; Song and Johnson, 2018; Vaquero-Sedas and Vega-Palas, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Marión et al., 2017; Platt et al., 2013; Song and Johnson, 2018; Vaquero-Sedas and Vega-Palas, 2019.

claim: Telomere dysfunction impairs stem cell differentiation in numerous contexts.
source: There are other consequences for cell fate beyond senescence, as telomere dysfunction is known to impair stem cell differentiation in numerous contexts (Harrington and Pucci, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Harrington and Pucci, 2018.

claim: Eroded telomeres in mESCs impair their ability to fully consolidate a differentiated phenotype in response to ATRA.
source: For example, eroded telomeres in mESCs impair their ability to fully consolidate a differentiated phenotype in response to all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) (Pucci et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Pucci et al., 2013.

claim: Repression of Nanog and Pou5f1 is impaired in late passage cells with critically short telomeres upon differentiation.
source: Repression of the pluripotency-promoting factors Nanog and Pou5f1 (also known as Oct4) is impaired in late passage cells with critically short telomeres upon differentiation, compared to wild-type (WT) or earlier passage telomerase-deficient (Tert-/-) mESCs with longer telomeres.
evidence: The claim is based on previously published work by the authors.

claim: The impairment in pluripotency gene repression in mESCs with dysfunctional telomeres is associated with a reduction in DNA methylation at the Nanog promoter.
source: This impairment is associated with a reduction in DNA methylation at the Nanog promoter (Pucci et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Pucci et al., 2013.

claim: The impaired repression of pluripotency genes in mESCs with dysfunctional telomeres is reversible.
source: The impaired repression of pluripotency genes in mESCs with dysfunctional telomeres is reversible, and telomere rescue via Tert reintroduction, or ectopic expression of Dnmt3b, elicits a partial reversal of this differentiation defect (Pucci et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Pucci et al., 2013.

claim: Telomere rescue via Tert reintroduction elicits a partial reversal of the differentiation defect in mESCs with dysfunctional telomeres.
source: The impaired repression of pluripotency genes in mESCs with dysfunctional telomeres is reversible, and telomere rescue via Tert reintroduction, or ectopic expression of Dnmt3b, elicits a partial reversal of this differentiation defect (Pucci et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Pucci et al., 2013.

claim: Ectopic expression of Dnmt3b elicits a partial reversal of the differentiation defect in mESCs with dysfunctional telomeres.
source: The impaired repression of pluripotency genes in mESCs with dysfunctional telomeres is reversible, and telomere rescue via Tert reintroduction, or ectopic expression of Dnmt3b, elicits a partial reversal of this differentiation defect (Pucci et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Pucci et al., 2013.

claim: The repression of Nanog and Pou5f1 during differentiation relies upon H3K27me3 deposition via PRC2.
source: Since the repression of Nanog and Pou5f1 during differentiation rely upon H3K27me3 deposition via the Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2) (Obier et al., 2015; Villasante et al., 2011), and Dnmt3 and PRC2 are critical to mESC neural differentiation (Liu et al., 2018), we investigated whether perturbation of H3K27me3 levels, genome-wide, could further impact the cell differentiation defect associated with dysfunctional telomeres.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Obier et al., 2015; Villasante et al., 2011.

claim: Dnmt3 and PRC2 are critical to mESC neural differentiation.
source: Since the repression of Nanog and Pou5f1 during differentiation rely upon H3K27me3 deposition via the Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2) (Obier et al., 2015; Villasante et al., 2011), and Dnmt3 and PRC2 are critical to mESC neural differentiation (Liu et al., 2018), we investigated whether perturbation of H3K27me3 levels, genome-wide, could further impact the cell differentiation defect associated with dysfunctional telomeres.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2018.

claim: Chemical modulators of histone H3K27 methylation specifically affect the fate of mESCs with short telomeres, with little effect on WT mESCs.
source: We found a striking ability of chemical modulators of histone H3K27 methylation to specifically affect the fate of mESCs with short telomeres, with little effect on WT mESCs.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with PRC2 and Kdm6a/b inhibitors shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Telomere status and histone methylation may be more linked than previously appreciated.
source: We suggest that telomere status and histone methylation may be more linked than previously appreciated.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing interdependency between telomere status and H3K27me3 modulation.

claim: The parental cell line used is E14 murine embryonic stem cells, derived from 129J.
source: The parental cell line used is E14 murine embryonic stem cells, derived from 129J.
evidence: The claim is a statement of the materials used in the study.

claim: The wild-type and Tert-/- ESCs were generated and described in Liu et al. (2000).
source: The wild-type and Tert-/- ESCs were generated and described in Liu et al. (2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Liu et al. (2000).

claim: UNC1999 and GSK343 are small competitive inhibitors of the Ezh2 co-factor S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) and are 1000-fold more selective over other Histone Methyl Transferases (HMT).
source: UNC1999 and GSK343 are small competitive inhibitors of the Ezh2 co-factor S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) and are 1000-fold more selective over other Histone Methyl Transferases (HMT).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about these chemical inhibitors.

claim: The major difference between UNC1999 and GSK343 is their inhibition selectivity for Ezh2 (compared to Ezh1), at 22- and 60-fold, respectively.
source: The major difference between UNC1999 and GSK343 is their inhibition selectivity for Ezh2 (compared to Ezh1), at 22- and 60-fold, respectively (https://www.thesgc.org/chemical-probes/GSK343; https://www.thesgc.org/chemical-probes/UNC1999), (Konze et al., 2013; Verma et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Konze et al., 2013; Verma et al., 2012 and references to SGC chemical probe information.

claim: A395 is an allosteric inhibitor of Eed that antagonizes binding to H3K27me3 and leads to impaired PRC2 function.
source: A395 was also employed as an allosteric inhibitor of Eed that antagonizes binding to H3K27me3 and leads to impaired PRC2 function (He et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to He et al., 2017.

claim: GSKJ4 is an inhibitor of H3K27me3 demethylase.
source: GSKJ4 is an inhibitor of H3K27me3 demethylase and GSKJ5 is a less potent, structurally related molecule (https://www.thesgc.org/chemical-probes/GSKJ1).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about GSKJ4 and reference to SGC chemical probe information.

claim: GSKJ5 is a less potent, structurally related molecule to GSKJ4.
source: GSKJ4 is an inhibitor of H3K27me3 demethylase and GSKJ5 is a less potent, structurally related molecule (https://www.thesgc.org/chemical-probes/GSKJ1).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about GSKJ5 and reference to SGC chemical probe information.
